This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.

papers.title: HME-PFD: Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation
papers.authors: Wen Xu, Xiaomin Zhang, Yucheng Yang, Danny Liu et al.
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, facilitating efficient serving of machine learning systems. In the context of ads recommendation, privileged features distillation (PFD) extends KD by allowing the teacher model to leverage privileged features, i.e., features available only during training, to enhance distillation performance. However, in real-world scenarios, privileged features often have limited coverage and exhibit heterogeneous distributions, resulting in training examples of varying importance for distillation and model learning. We propose Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation (HME-PFD), a novel approach that incorporates privileged features into the routing module of a Mixture-of-Experts-based student model. Our method introduces both hard-coded and learnable routing modules, enabling the student to dynamically determine expert assignment based on the availability and values of privileged features. This design allows the student model to better handle the heterogeneous data scenario, where privileged features are partially observed, by differentiating between high- and low-signal samples. Extensive experiments on two post-click conversion prediction tasks demonstrate that HME-PFD consistently outperforms baseline methods. Our results show that leveraging privileged features for expert routing in the student model leads to improved model performance, even when privileged features are incomplete or sparse.

papers.title: Spoof Localization as Boundary Regression
papers.authors: Yixuan Xiao, Xin Wang, Yassine El Kheir, Feidi Kallel et al.
papers.summary: Partially spoofed audio embeds spoofed segments in a bonafide utterance, and spoof localization is the task of locating them. Most countermeasures (CMs) operate at the frame level. Typically, they include a front-end representing the audio as frames and a back-end classifying each frame as bonafide or spoof. Such frame-level detection ties the reference, the predictions and the evaluation to a pre-defined temporal resolution: a frame containing a transition receives a single label, a boundary cannot lie inside a frame, and the evaluation also depends on the resolution. To tackle these issues, we treat spoof localization as regression. We propose a single-stage boundary regressor that outputs (start-time, end-time, score) tuples with continuous-valued time stamps, trained on the exact reference intervals. Results show that the proposed CM outperforms previous frame-level and boundary-based CMs, and generalizes better.

papers.title: Projecting Beauty: Transferring Image Aesthetic Analysis onto 3D Heritage and Urban Scenes
papers.authors: Sophia Kovalenko, Alexander M. Rusnak, Vittoria Meroni, Yasmine Kroknes-Gomez et al.
papers.summary: Judgments about the beauty of buildings and streets inform architectural design, urban planning, and heritage conservation, yet increasingly rely on scanned 3D models over material fabric. Automatic aesthetic assessment remains largely confined to 2D photographs. We ask what survives when image aesthetic assessment crosses this dimensional gap to produce dense, per-point aesthetic descriptions of heritage and urban point clouds. We examine three routes that sidestep costly, and sometimes ethically dubious, human labeling at scale: (1) lifting scalar scores from image aesthetic models (NIMA, SAAN) onto geometry; (2) training Aesthetic Visual Analysis (AVA) regression heads on frozen vision backbones (DINOv3, TIPS, SigLIP2, PE, RADSeg) or, in a 3D-native variant, a generalist point encoder on feed-forward AVA reconstructions; and (3) querying lifted vision-language features with a natural-language aesthetic label, taking similarity as a score. The two supervised routes transfer poorly: heads fitting AVA in-domain produce architectural class profiles that neither reproduce one another nor track other signals, while the 3D-native probe stays near chance due to reconstruction geometry quality. Text querying is markedly more coherent. Projecting out the class-text direction from point features raises mean cross-model agreement on architectural part profiles from +0.035 to +0.352, and from +0.113 to +0.293 per point; the four backbones passing a semantic sanity check correlate at 0.31-0.73, while the failing one remains an outlier. Since model agreement is not agreement with human aesthetic perception, we detail a part-aware rating protocol to clarify where human and automatic ratings disagree. We provide a reproducible transfer protocol, an account of which pseudo-labeling routes carry signal, and dense aesthetic pseudo-labels meant as hypotheses rather than ground truth.

papers.title: ViewPACT: Multi-View Geometric Augmentation and Pose-Action Co-Training for Viewpoint-Robust Manipulation
papers.authors: Chenglang Tu, Feng Chen, Ruizhe Liu, Pei Zhou et al.
papers.summary: Image policies are scalable but remain brittle to camera viewpoint changes. On LIBERO, we identify proprioception as an input shortcut: masking robot states sharply degrades several policies, while retraining from images alone recovers much of the loss. We introduce ViewPACT, an image policy trained with privileged geometric supervision. Auxiliary objectives recover end-effector and task-relevant object poses in the camera frame, while deployment requires only RGB observations. Joint geometric supervision improves mean simulation success from 37.4% to 78.4% under unseen external-camera viewpoints, with more modest gains under separately evaluated object, scene, and camera-intrinsic shifts. Across four real-robot tasks, combining simulated and real-image geometric supervision achieves 68.1% mean success, versus 3.1% for fixed-view behavior cloning and 30.6% for the strongest evaluated alternative. These results support geometric supervision for viewpoint robustness in the evaluated fixed-view demonstration setting.

papers.title: HiPerfCC-StateReuse: Ciphertext Reuse for Fast Confidential GPU Data Movement
papers.authors: Haoxuan Xu, Shaoyu Wang, Minghao Lin, Beijie Liu et al.
papers.summary: Confidential GPUs offer near-native on-device compute performance, but transfers between CPU and GPU TEEs through untrusted host memory require bulk CPU encryption and decryption, even for unchanged data. Existing software techniques overlap or parallelize these operations but retain their per-byte CPU cost. Reusing exported ciphertext could avoid this work, but GPU TEE firmware enforces direction-specific encryption keys and fresh per-transfer initialization vectors (IVs), preventing direct reuse. We introduce ciphertext rebinding, a purely software primitive enabling repeated and cross-GPU ciphertext reuse on existing GPU TEEs without hardware changes, while preserving confidentiality, integrity, and freshness. Specifically, ciphertext rebinding exploits the separation between ciphertext-dependent and IV-dependent components in GPU TEE's AES-GCM authentication: a GPU-precomputed summary under the destination key can enable the CPU to update authentication tags without processing the payload. With this modification, GPU's subsequent read on the retained ciphertext can still proceed through the GPU's hardware-fixed copy-engine interfaces, which cannot be modified by software. An additional GPU correction step can then compensate for differences in the keys and IVs to recover the original plaintext. By retaining GPU-exported ciphertext in untrusted host memory, ciphertext rebinding avoids bulk CPU decryption and re-encryption, improving effective bandwidth for GPU-state restoration and sharing. We implement this primitive in HiPerfCC-StateReuse through only driver and library changes, combining batched submissions with pipelined GPU processing and copy-engine transfers. We evaluate transfer efficiency and CPU overhead through microbenchmarks, and application performance through three case studies: model switching, key-value cache offloading, and cross-instance cache sharing.

papers.title: RES: Accelerating Diffusion Language Models with Rolling Entropy Sampling
papers.authors: Patrick Pynadath, Nicolas Perez-Nieves, Bobak Shahriari, Jean Tarbouriech et al.
papers.summary: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.

papers.title: Single-Transformer Latent Diffusion
papers.authors: Hao-Yu Hsu, Shenlong Wang, Alexander G. Schwing
papers.summary: Latent generative models typically rely on three separate networks: an encoder that tokenizes pixels, a generator that models the latent distribution, and a decoder that maps latents back to pixels. UNITE recently merged the first two into a single generative encoder trained in one stage, but its decoder remains a separate network. We ask whether this last network can be folded in too, so that one diffusion transformer encodes, generates, and decodes. Simply letting the shared backbone decode does not help. What makes it work is to cast all three modes as position-aligned sequence maps over one fully shared backbone, distinguished only by a mode token and the timestep. The resulting model, UNIFIED, is simple: one network trained from scratch in a single stage with only reconstruction and flow-matching losses, without adversarial losses or pretrained encoders (e.g., DINO). On ImageNet-1K 256x256 at matched parameters, UNIFIED improves gFID over UNITE at three sizes ( 60M, 115M, and 215M) and reaches 2.08 with 215M parameters, the lowest among compared models under 250M parameters. On text-to-image generation, UNIFIED-B (218M) reaches a GenEval score of 0.87 at 512x512, exceeding single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters. Full unification of latent diffusion is thus not merely feasible but beneficial.

papers.title: BO-COMM: Bidirectional Optical System for Simultaneous Localization and Communication in Swarm Robotics
papers.authors: Cheng Hu, Haotian Wu, Qi Lin, Manrui Zheng et al.
papers.summary: Swarm robotics experiments require observations of robot pose and operational state, together with mechanisms for returning environmental information to the robots. Shared channel wireless communication can face contention and congestion as concurrent reporting demands increase, while a static visual marker does not itself convey changing robot states. We present BO-COMM, an optical system that combines pose estimation and dynamic state reporting with optical downstream interaction. A camera observes circular LED arrays mounted on Colias IV robots with CEU-PLUS extension units.Ring-based voting estimates robot centers, and the spatial LED pattern provides orientation and an encoded state. A projector supplies spatial environmental cues, while an infrared module provides a separate command channel. Processing-time measurements, path-following and color-reporting experiments, and a multi-pheromone demonstration illustrate the operation of this architecture in a planar arena. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining optical pose and state observations with environmental feedback in the tested hardware and arena configuration.

papers.title: Speech Emotion Recognition Across Languages: Prosodic Patterns and Self-Supervised Learning
papers.authors: Tianqi Geng, Zhichen Han, Hui Feng, Jiahong Yuan et al.
papers.summary: This study investigates the prosodic patterns of emotional speech across Chinese (CN), German (DE), and English (EN), with a focus on acoustic characteristics. Using ANOVA and mixed-effects modeling, we reveal cross-linguistic and emotion-specific prosodic patterns. A comparative analysis of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) performance demonstrates that humans outperform Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) models in cross-lingual tasks, while SSL models show significant improvement in cross-lingual SER through an efficient fine-tuning process, achieving performance competitive with native human speakers. The study also analyzes the performance of Speech Emotion Diarization (SED) between models and humans, highlighting the effectiveness of SSL models in transfer learning scenarios. These findings emphasize the interplay between universal prosodic features (e.g., intensity, pitch) and language-specific factors. Moreover, the SSL model's outstanding performance indicates the potential value of these acoustic features in emotion processing, implying possible advancements in cross-lingual emotion recognition through refined training techniques.

papers.title: Distributed Interactive Conformal Prediction for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Daniel M. Cherenson, Dimitra Panagou
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems increasingly rely on learning-enabled components and distributed algorithms for perception, estimation, and control, introducing uncertainty that makes it challenging to satisfy mission requirements. Conformal prediction quantifies uncertainty with distribution-free guarantees, but existing methods do not address the challenging combination of dependence among robots, distributed calibration, and the distribution shift induced when calibrated uncertainty bounds modify the closed-loop system. We introduce Multi-Agent Interactive Conformal Prediction (MA-ICP), a distributed framework for computing robustness margins in heterogeneous systems to satisfy mission requirements with high probability. MA-ICP aggregates robot-level nonconformity scores, which measure errors in modeled or estimated quantities, into one mission-level score per robot class, allowing dependence among robots within each mission. Mission-level scores and quantiles are computed using neighbor-to-neighbor communication in a finite number of communication rounds. Updating the robustness margins changes robot trajectories and distributed algorithm outputs, so we use class-dependent score sensitivities to upper bound the shift in mission-level scores. We then establish calibration-conditional coverage guarantees per robot class for the updated margins. We demonstrate MA-ICP on cooperative payload control, formation control with obstacle avoidance, and distributed target tracking missions.

papers.title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM
papers.authors: Felix Desyatirikov
papers.summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

papers.title: SenFabric: 3D Printing On-fabric Sensing Mechanisms for Smart Textiles
papers.authors: Yao Wang, Mingming Li, Vera Yu Wu, Marwa AlAlawi et al.
papers.summary: We present SenFabric, a one-step fabrication technique that 3D prints conductive TPU directly onto existing fabric. Rather than compensating for conductive material instability, SenFabric uses geometry-driven resistive structures in which motion changes conductive contact and reconfigures the effective path, producing characteristic signal responses that remain distinguishable despite variation in absolute resistance. We introduce four sensing primitives, slide, press, stretch, and bend, with geometric variables that control activation force, deformation range, and resolution, and a browser-based tool that adapts them to user-supplied outlines and generates routing, pins, and printable models. Four applications demonstrate wearable sensing, human-robot interaction, garment interfaces, and animal wearables, while evaluations show geometry-dominated sensing, cross-motion selectivity, and stable response under repeated use.

papers.title: From Spatial Perception to Speech Recovery: Binaural Semantic Adaptation for Spatially Grounded Multi-Talker Transcription
papers.authors: Wenxuan He, Shan Liang
papers.summary: Spatial audio large language models increasingly combine general audio understanding with spatial perception. Yet overlapping conversations require more than locating speakers. A model must also recover what each person says and match the words to their positions. We examine this challenge in MiDashengLM-Spatial, a binaural model designed for both spatial reasoning and general audio understanding. To test these abilities, we introduce BiCP-Bench, a benchmark of overlapping two-speaker binaural recordings that contrasts candidate-based recognition, position-guided transcription, and joint transcription with spatial attribution. The model can identify a target utterance among candidates but struggles to transcribe it without them. Its semantic encoder uses only one ear. Changing that ear shifts which side's speech is recovered more accurately, despite unchanged binaural input to the spatial branch. We therefore propose Binaural Semantic Adaptation (BiSA), which combines shared encoding of both ears with cross-ear differential interactions. With the backbone frozen and 0.027% trainable parameters, BiSA raises correctly attributed joint transcription success from 0% to 57.81% for simultaneous onsets. For staggered onsets, later-speaker word error rate falls from 109.47% to 29.58%. On full-length Clarity CEC1 mixtures, word error rate falls from 59.33% to 39.60%. Spatial reasoning on MMAU-Pro improves by 9.54 percentage points without updating the spatial encoder, and general audio performance remains largely intact.

papers.title: graspit-py: A Python Interface to GraspIt! for Grasp Planning Under Pose and Friction Uncertainty
papers.authors: Clinton Enwerem, John S. Baras, Calin Belta
papers.summary: In simulated multifingered grasps, pose error can change contacts formed during hand closure, while friction uncertainty changes the loads supported by those contacts. Existing C++ APIs and ROS 1 services provide programmatic GraspIt! access but require native bindings or a service transport layer for Python use and application-specific integration of contact geometry with uncertainty sampling. A Python workflow for these studies must connect native closure and contacts to caller-defined wrench scores, uncertainty samples, and command reconstruction. We present graspit-py, a Python interface to native GraspIt! operations that supplies this workflow. The interface provides native scene access, contact-wrench analysis, and configurable approach planning under pose and friction uncertainty. A grasp record associates the object-relative palm pose and closed independent coordinates with nominal contacts and quality scores evaluated under sampled pose and friction conditions. Our MuJoCo exporter derives serial hinge chains and affine joint couplings, including nonzero reference angles, and preserves individual collision components. Across 75 configurations of five hand models, maximum discrepancy between source and exported palm-frame vertex sets was approximately 1.3 micrometers against a 100-micrometer geometry tolerance. We isolated reference-angle and collision-component effects through controlled ablations and validated 1,920 directional task-wrench capacity calculations against independent Cartesian-force linear programs. In a common GraspIt! workload, median reset-close-score-state cycle latency through direct Python was 10.7% lower than through persistent ROS 1 services. An executable export-plan-reconstruct workflow and grasp examples on six hand models demonstrate how the contact, score, and joint representations support numerical analysis and command reconstruction.

papers.title: Consumer-Time Validity in Stateful AI Runtimes: Verifying Recovered State and Deferred Authority
papers.authors: Guijia Zhang, Huihao Jing, Bing Li, Shing-Chi Cheung et al.
papers.summary: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.

papers.title: "What Should I Do?" Guidelines for Responsibly Integrating AI in Software Engineering
papers.authors: Rudrajit Choudhuri, Fatima A. Moussaoui, Carmen Badea, Christian Bird et al.
papers.summary: Speculations abound about the "right" ways for developers to integrate AI into their software engineering (SE) work, but the evidence that exists is sparse and contradictory. Yet, developers are held responsible for the products they ship with (or without) AI's help, so they need to integrate AI in responsible ways. To address this gap, we conducted a two-phase, large-scale investigation with 1,118 developers at Microsoft, GitHub, and Pfizer. In Phase 1, we surveyed 860 developers at Microsoft on where they sought and resisted AI support in their daily work, and from their accounts, synthesized 35 developer-facing guidelines: 29 across five categories of SE work and 6 cross-cutting ones. A year later, as AI capabilities and developers' experiences co-evolved, we validated them in Phase 2 with 258 developers in technology (Microsoft, GitHub) and biopharmaceutical (Pfizer) domains. Developers in our study found the guidelines clearly worded (92%) and relevant to their work (91%), and most wanted to adopt them in their own work (89%). We also report how developers described operationalizing these guidelines in practice: using AI to refine their craft and delegate verifiable work, while keeping judgment and accountability for themselves. For relationship-centric work, endorsement varied with developers' domain and their SE and AI experience. Overall, we offer concrete advice from in-the-trenches developers to other in-the-trenches developers, and a shared vocabulary that engineering teams can adopt to integrate AI well in their work.

papers.title: MB-SSIM: A Multi-Band Variant of SSIM, Tunable to Viewing Conditions
papers.authors: Yuriy A. Reznik
papers.summary: SSIM, as practically deployed, contains a hidden two-band model: although it was introduced as a departure from channel-based vision models, it amounts to a product of one similarity functional applied to a low-pass and a high-pass version of the two images. This split, however, is defined in pixels, so the spatial frequencies each band covers, as seen by the viewer, change with the display and the viewing distance. Making the model explicit and expressing it in cycles per degree gives a version of SSIM that takes the viewing conditions into account while preserving its simplicity. The resulting metric, MB-SSIM, keeps SSIM's per-patch product of similarity ratios; the bands are placed where psychophysics places the visual system's channels, and the viewing geometry enters through a single number, the angular sampling density in pixels per degree. On the CID:IQ dataset, which rates the same 690 images at two viewing distances, one set of sub-band weights fitted jointly and evaluated on held-out content reaches a pooled PLCC of 0.834 against 0.787 for SSIM and 0.808 for MS-SSIM; on LIVE Release 2, calibrating the geometry yields 0.956 against 0.946 and 0.950. As a cross-verification, the CID:IQ weights applied unchanged to the Brightcove-Kingston multi-screen video dataset, which rates the same clips on a television, a tablet and a phone, give a pooled PLCC of 0.844 across devices where SSIM and MS-SSIM, which must return one number per clip, fall to 0.62 and 0.59. Accuracy is flat from three channels to six and insensitive to filter shape, window and peak placement; only the channel bandwidths matter, and the psychophysically measured values are a safe choice. The most sensitive parameter is SSIM's own stabilising constant: reducing it to a third raises the pooled PLCC to 0.857. Source code reproducing the results is available.

papers.title: Micro Operational Robustness of LLMs on Code Generation
papers.authors: Debalina Ghosh Paul, Hong Zhu, Ian Bayley
papers.summary: It is now common practice in software development for large language models (LLMs) to be used to generate program code. It is desirable to evaluate the robustness of LLMs for this usage. This paper is concerned in particular with how sensitive LLMs are to variations in descriptions of the coding tasks. However, existing techniques for evaluating this robustness are unsuitable for code generation because the input data space of natural language (NL) descriptions is discrete and sparse. To address this problem, we propose a robustness evaluation method called scenario domain analysis, which aims to find the expected minimal change in the NL descriptions of coding tasks that would cause the LLMs to produce incorrect outputs. We have formally proved the theoretical properties of the method and also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of four state-of-the-art LLMs: Gemini-pro, Codex, Llamma2 and Falcon 7B, and have found that we are able to rank these with confidence from best to worst. Moreover, we have also studied how robustness varies in different scenarios, including the variations with the topic of the coding task and with the complexity of its sample solution, and found that robustness is lower for more complex tasks and also lower for more advanced topics, such as multi-threading and data structures.

papers.title: ActWithin: Bounding Wrong-Payment Risk in Delegated Payment Batches
papers.authors: Shuhao Zheng, Zhipeng Wang, Zi Xuan Zhang, Yang Huang
papers.summary: A delegated payment agent can hold valid rights for incompatible revisions of a batch. We study the window in which the selected revision cannot be verified by the execution deadline. For batches that permit every subset of up to q revisions, ActWithin compiles the limit into a shared quota of q successful replacement payments. If approved plans are mutually replayable with the same observable inputs, deadlines, and resources, this quota preserves normal completion without additional approvals and minimizes worst-case wrong-payment principal for arbitrary positive amounts. A dynamic program computes its exact risk and witness. For amount-preserving recipient changes, we derive the exact risk of the tightest single amount cap on the same replacement group, provided mixed payment subsets can settle within the window. A two-phase result isolates the risk to payments due before trusted verification. Against the amount cap, an exploratory setting with 16-64 payments and one quarter of positions revisable yields aggregate reductions of 16.23-16.88% on adapted IBM AMLSim amounts and 10.12-12.52% on an adapted controlled catalog. The 760 funded original controlled paths with constructed single-position revisions yield 2.69%. In one local MetaMask fixture, both policies complete all 37 normal plans and the worst wrong debit falls from 93,962 to 81,056 test wei.

papers.title: Intrinsic Value Modules: Trusted-Hardware Support for Locally Final Offline Asset Transfer
papers.authors: AmirReza Fathi, Ali Rahimi
papers.summary: Consensus lets distributed participants agree on a common state, but it makes monetary validity depend on network connectivity and collective acceptance. We explore making validity intrinsic to a digital coin. We propose an Intrinsic Value Module (IVM): trusted hardware that gives a coin locally verifiable authenticity and spendability, analogous to verifying a signature. Under stated hardware and cryptographic assumptions, the IVM abstraction and our offline transfer protocol move monetary uniqueness from a replicated ledger into non-clonable protected state. The protocol prevents forgery, replay, double credit, and double spending by genuine, uncompromised IVMs; communication failures may lock value but cannot duplicate it. We distinguish local transfer atomicity and asset uniqueness, which the protocol establishes, from global state consistency across disconnected devices, which it does not. The IVM does not eliminate trust; it relocates trust to certified hardware, issuer roots, and non-rollback state. We present the architecture, protocol, and security analysis, and discuss open challenges.

papers.title: Ads for Agents: Measuring Ad-Serving MCP Servers
papers.authors: Shahrooz Pouryousef, Sohini Chakraborty, Ali Montazer, Muoi Tran
papers.summary: AI agents call external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Some MCP servers return paid advertisements (ads) into the model's context. The model then decides whether these ads and their disclosures reach the user. We trace these ads from their sources to the agent's tool results across public MCP servers and packages. We find the servers through their public traces in ad networks, package registries, certificate logs, hostnames, MCP directories, and GitHub configurations. We then query the ad-serving servers with read-only requests and inspect their ad links. Ads appear on only 0.57% of 101,363 open MCP endpoints and 0.04% of 122,656 local MCP packages. Although 173 ad networks target agents, operators insert the ads themselves on about half of the 226 ad-returning servers. Nearly all ad-serving packages likewise carry the operator's own affiliate identifier. While ads adapt to the topic and intent of the query, their disclosure stays fixed within each tool. Only 9.3% of the ads carry an explicit sponsored label. Most ad links also hide their destinations. Since operators insert most ads themselves and label them inconsistently, we propose a per-item ad annotation in MCP results. Clients can show this annotation to the user independently of the model's answer.

papers.title: Health Ikigai: Semantic Conversational Interfaces for Wearable Health Data to Support Behavioral Change for Senior Indian
papers.authors: Md Haseen Akhtar, Hansoo Lee, Rafael A. Calvo
papers.summary: In ubiquitous health contexts, wearable feedback is often encountered in brief, interrupted moments of everyday life. However, many wearable and mobile health systems still present personal health data through numerical dashboards, leaving users and health coaches to interpret trends, thresholds, and deviations on their own. This interpretive burden may be especially relevant for adults aged 50-65 in India, where digital literacy, health literacy, language, and daily routines can shape how health technologies are understood and used. We present Health Ikigai, a design-oriented proof-of-concept framework that reframes wearable activity feedback from dashboard-based numerical interpretation to semantic conversational feedback. The prototype transforms replayed wearable-derived activity data into baseline-aware triggers, plain-language feedback, limited-turn conversational prompts, and coach-facing review summaries. A preliminary formative evaluation with ten adults in India suggests that participants perceived the interaction as understandable, lightweight, supportive, and actionable. We discuss design implications for low-burden wearable health interfaces that preserve coach oversight while reducing users' interpretive work.

papers.title: Postpartum Sense-Making and AI in a Fragmented Care System
papers.authors: Diana Freed, Maja Mishevska
papers.summary: Postpartum women must navigate health information across a fragmented landscape of clinicians, peers, online communities, influencers, and, increasingly, large language models (LLMs). Existing evaluations of LLMs in health contexts primarily ask whether systems provide accurate, safe, and readable information. We argue that these criteria, while essential, are insufficient for understanding how LLMs may affect postpartum care. LLMs enter an information ecology in which women are already required to reconcile competing forms of expertise, determine whether their experiences are normal or concerning, and decide when and where to seek care. At the same time, online representations of motherhood and femininity shape which postpartum experiences are made visible and what forms of self-management are expected of women. Drawing together research on postpartum care gaps, online help-seeking, influencer cultures, gendered responsibility, and AI-supported health information, we position LLMs as emerging intermediaries within this broader care infrastructure. We argue that evaluating postpartum AI requires examining not only information quality, but also how these systems shape epistemic coordination, transitions to formal care, and the distribution of responsibility for making fragmented systems of care work.

papers.title: Restorable Multilingual Voice Anonymization via Audio Watermarking
papers.authors: Haoyuan Zheng, Guang Hua, Xiaoxiao Miao
papers.summary: Voice anonymization aims to conceal speaker identity while preserving linguistic and paralinguistic information. However, certain applications also require the ability to attribute anonymized recordings to their original speakers. Existing recovery approaches often rely on specially designed reversible anonymization systems, limiting their applicability to different anonymization architectures. In this work, we propose a post-hoc framework for restorable multilingual voice anonymization that enables speaker attribution without reconstructing the original waveform or modifying the underlying anonymization systems. Specifically, we convert 192-dimensional speaker embeddings into binary identity payloads through sign quantization and embed them into anonymized speech using a segment-wise audio watermarking strategy. Recovered payloads are subsequently matched against enrollment speaker templates for identity attribution. We evaluate the framework across four languages using two distinct anonymization backbones, BM1 and T24. Under clean conditions, the approach achieves approximately 99% exact payload recovery and 0.96% attribution EER while largely preserving the original privacy-utility performance. Experiments further show that speaker attribution remains reliable under several audio distortions despite imperfect payload recovery, although temporal rescaling severely disrupts recovery. Additional analyses reveal that watermark robustness varies across languages, carrier durations, and anonymization backbones.

papers.title: "I feel like AI is just everywhere": A longitudinal qualitative study on parents' perceptions, use, and mediation of GenAI
papers.authors: Jennica Li, Shirley Zhang, Dakota Sullivan, Bilge Mutlu et al.
papers.summary: GenAI has developed rapidly over the last few years, yet few longitudinal studies exploring how individuals' experiences with GenAI have changed over time exist. Even fewer studies have focused on families with children, despite the opportunity to explore how parents have balanced their needs, their children's development, and the fast pace in which technology changes. To better understand how parents' perceptions, use, and mediation of GenAI shifted over two years, we interviewed 10 parents who had participated in a prior study about their families' experiences with GenAI. Parents had shifted from thinking GenAI was novel to feeling like it was unavoidable, characterizing GenAI as a limited tool to believing GenAI development needed to be regulated, and focusing on their personal mediation strategies to wanting systemic plans to curb GenAI's long-term consequences. We position our findings within the context of parental mediation of technology and increasing collective mitigation of GenAI-related risks.

papers.title: Learning How a Body Moves: Few-Shot Body Inference for Visual World Models of Animated Characters
papers.authors: Amarnath R
papers.summary: Two visually identical animated characters can respond differently to the same action command because their body dynamics differ. For example, a stiff blob and its bouncy twin reach different heights when both receive the jump command. Given only the first frame and the action command, a visual world model has no information to distinguish these twins, because their initial appearances are identical. We therefore propose an in-context world model that encodes clips of a character's other actions into a body representation, using a contrastive loss to separate look-alike characters. We introduce ToonTwins, a benchmark of 144 2D cartoon characters that run, jump, fall, turn and crouch. Its characters form look-alike groups of four that differ only in their dynamics profile, and we also evaluate the model on 32 animated animals from DeformingThings4D. Even with a body code from these clips, the latent pixel world model we tested recovered at most 25 percent of the twins' jump height difference. On new shapes, our model identified the correct twin in 85.9 percent of cases, compared with 76.7 percent for a transformer baseline that reads the same clips without a body summary, and in a controlled ablation the contrastive loss gave more than half of this gain. On the animated animals, it reduced the mean path prediction error by 8.5 percent against a model without body information.

papers.title: Beyond Raw IQ: Compact Semantic Representations for Task Oriented Automatic Modulation Classification
papers.authors: Omm Swarup, Shrishail M. Hiremath
papers.summary: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is an important component of modern wireless communication systems, but conventional signal representations can be expensive to store, process, and communicate, particularly under noisy channel conditions. This work investigates whether learned semantic representations can provide a compact alternative to high-dimensional in-phase and quadrature (IQ) representations while retaining robustness to noise. Starting from a 2048-dimensional IQ representation, we evaluate learned semantic representations with dimensions of 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64. Across the evaluated configurations, a 16-dimensional representation provides the strongest overall trade-off between classification performance, robustness, and representation size. The resulting representation achieves a 128x compression ratio and a 99.22% reduction in dimensionality. We further evaluate representation stability across signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), compare semantic representations with a raw-IQ CNN, analyze per-class robustness, and perform five-seed validation. The five-seed evaluation produces an average accuracy of (49.22 +- 0.52)% and Macro-F1 of (49.27 +- 0.53)% across the evaluated SNR range. These results indicate that learned semantic compression can produce a substan- tially smaller representation while preserving useful classification information and improving geometric stability under noise.

papers.title: Dhaani: A Data-Flow-Driven Tool for Greenfield Construction and Brownfield Modernisation
papers.authors: Shraddha Surana, Ashwin Srinivasan
papers.summary: Large language models can generate plausible code quickly, but an end-to-end prompt leaves developers with little control over decomposition, interfaces, or the assumptions that must survive later revisions. We present Dhaani, a free desktop application for greenfield program construction and brownfield repository modernisation. It makes an annotated data-flow diagram (ADFD) the inspectable contract between intent and implementation. In the greenfield workflow, Build, a user turns natural-language requirements into a typed graph, reviews process specifications and pre/post-conditions, ratifies generated modules, and proceeds in dependency order for Python or .NET (C#). In the brownfield workflow, Migrate uses source inference to recover an ADFD from a Fortran repository, performs target generation in bounded dependency groups, and exposes source-target alignment, generated code, errors, time, token use, and cost. The tool keeps code and artifacts on the user's machine and supports cloud or locally hosted models. Two scientific synthesis case studies produced executable systems where matched low/no-code baselines failed or were substantially less accurate. On 50 open-source Fortran repositories, the migration workflow made all 382 fixed source-oracle probes runnable and passed 327 (85.6%); two direct translation baselines each passed 83 (21.7% of planned probes). Pre-built installers and usage instructions are freely available. Tool and usage guide: https://shraddhasurana.github.io/dhaani/. Video: https://youtu.be/SShWwOMgJ9c.

papers.title: STAC++: Plug-and-Play Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Aware Cache Compression for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
papers.authors: Boyi Zhu, Youcheng Cai, Dong Wang
papers.summary: Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC's fixed-resolution spatial key-value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

papers.title: Beyond File-Level Splits: Rethinking Symbolic Music Evaluation via Multi-View Alignment
papers.authors: Kun Bai, Yinghan Wang, Canran Xiao, Jiachen Luo et al.
papers.summary: Symbolic music generation often continues MIDI passages by predicting subsequent notes or events. Held-out prediction loss can overestimate generalization to unseen compositions when training contains another performance or arrangement of a test work. We introduce Multi-View Alignment-Aware Same-Work Identification, combining complementary musical representations with temporal alignment of shared passages to remove test-work versions from training while preserving unrelated material and fixing evaluation files. In a controlled cohort of 100 manually verified pairs selected for high embedding similarity, replacing 3.29% of training windows with test-work versions reduces mean per-group NLL by up to 30.16% relative to matched unrelated content. Across two datasets and two generators, our method brings test losses closest to a reference built from independent work labels. Compared with removing the same number of files at random, it leaves fewer test works exposed and retains more eligible content, including about 99% of eligible tokens on the piano-performance dataset. A separate study on that dataset matches training tokens and updates: no test works remain exposed under the dataset labels, and mean relative test loss is 2.15% higher than an independently selected reference. These findings support keeping all versions of each composition in one split when evaluating generalization to unseen works. The project is available at https://kunbai05-nb.github.io/.

papers.title: Multimodal LLMs Know the Game but Assume the Real World
papers.authors: Jianxin Gao, Bohan Chen, Runze Li, Qi Zhang
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models can state the rules of a video game, but do they apply them when they only see the game? We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. Their errors pick the real-world outcome, the gap is largest where the game leaves a scene unchanged, and reasoning traces state the game's rule, then answer by reality. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.

papers.title: Routing Collapse in Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts: Cross-Modal Conditioning Restores Expert Diversity Without Improving Accuracy
papers.authors: Syed Hussamuddin, Mubashra Fayyaz
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifiers are increasingly applied to multimodal emotion recognition, yet the health of their routing distributions is rarely measured. We study a seven-expert MoE head on IEMOCAP under two conditions that differ only in how modality embeddings are fused before reaching it: a learned scalar gate alone, and the same gate preceded by pairwise cross-modal attention. Under scalar fusion the router collapses, concentrating on 1.88 of seven experts at a normalised entropy of 0.241. Cross-modal fusion raises entropy to 0.537 and utilisation to 3.25 experts, a 2.23x increase (p=0.035, Cohen's d=2.55), and induces emotion-differentiated routing absent in the scalar case. This recovered diversity confers no detectable benefit: across six seeds per condition, weighted accuracy (p=0.646) and run-to-run variance (p=0.768) are statistically indistinguishable. We further observe a 13-point accuracy spread under identical configuration. In this regime, router health and task performance are decoupled, and diagnosing collapse does not by itself justify fixing it.

papers.title: SkillLens: An Interactive Human-LLM System for Diagnosing and Refining Agent Skills
papers.authors: Shuo Yan, Rui Sheng, Xiaoyan Gu, Lian Lian et al.
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills, yet maintaining them requires developers to connect revisions with changes in behavior and task outcomes. Existing workflows fragment evidence across versions, evaluation cases, and execution traces. We present SkillLens, an interactive human-LLM system for diagnosing and refining agent skills. A formative study with five developers and researchers identified challenges in prioritizing failures, reconstructing case-level evidence, and preserving context across revisions. SkillLens links performance changes, case transitions, skill diffs, invocation sequences, traces, and outputs in a recoverable workflow, while keeping model-generated explanations and refinements under human review. Through a between-subjects user study with 20 participants, we show that SkillLens supports developers in diagnosing and refining agent skills through a more usable and less demanding workflow than the baseline. These findings highlight the value of linking version comparisons, case-level evidence, and human-reviewed refinement across skill iterations.

papers.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
papers.authors: Tobias Philipp
papers.summary: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.

papers.title: IndexerStage: Staging Indexer-K across Memory Tiers for Sparse-Attention LLM Serving
papers.authors: Xin Zhang, Weifeng Zhang, Xianyan Xie, Huijun Shen et al.
papers.summary: Long-context sparse-attention serving can remain limited by graphics processing unit (GPU) memory after attention data is offloaded. DeepSeek Sparse Attention retains Indexer-K state to select the tokens that attention will read. Its indexer scans this growing state in full at every layer and decode step. A full scan requires the current layer's state, however, not simultaneous residency of every layer. We present IndexerStage, a serving runtime that externalizes Indexer-K state while preserving native GPU score, top-k, and attention kernels. It stages completed pages through shared execution buffers and preserves new entries locally. Joint memory-and-transfer admission checks storage and each layer's transfer demand before accepting a growing batch. The backing tier gathers pages; the model-serving GPU controls transfer timing and byte budgets. We implement IndexerStage in SGLang on 16 model-serving and 16 backing H800 GPUs. Across 16K–64K inputs, local streaming storage occupies 0.65–0.70 GiB per model-serving GPU. Relative to host-memory-backed HiSparse, batch size increases by 12.28–23.08% and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS) reaches 1.08–1.14x. At 64K with the latent-KV backing path fixed, the larger batch achieves 1.10x decode TPS; enabling streaming at batch size 24 adds 2.42% to time per output token. Mixed-length dynamic serving increases mean generating batch size by 12.07% and delivers 1.31x decode TPS.

papers.title: Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
papers.authors: Leizhen Zhang, Sheng Chen
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.

papers.title: Making Repeated Variational Circuit Optimization Efficient on GPUs
papers.authors: Runzhe Zhang, Jiaqi Liu, Anbang Wu, Pu Pang et al.
papers.summary: Repeated numerical optimization is a defining workload for classical simulation of parameterized quantum circuits. Although successive training steps change gate parameters, they usually preserve circuit connectivity and reuse a small set of gate-layer patterns. We use this regularity to accelerate gradient evaluation on GPUs. Our framework combines execution primitives for common circuit layers with adjoint differentiation, coordinating state evolution and derivative computation to reduce launch overhead, intermediate storage, and state-vector traffic. Because effective schedules depend on circuit size, gate structure, and device resources, our framework retains several execution choices instead of committing to a single schedule. Structural and hardware constraints narrow these choices, after which measurements on representative layers guide plan selection. The selected plans are reused while circuit structure remains fixed, spreading the selection cost over repeated training iterations. This approach targets the computation required by optimization rather than forward simulation alone, while retaining the numerical semantics of state-vector differentiation. Experiments across multiple circuit families and GPU platforms compare our framework with the native GPU adjoint implementation in PennyLane Lightning. The results demonstrate substantially lower gradient evaluation times over the evaluated workloads, together with the numerical accuracy checks reported in the evaluation.

papers.title: CCAMoE: Cache-Conditioned Adaptive Inference for Offloaded MoE
papers.authors: Xuan Zhang, Haisheng Tan, Han Tian, Jialiang Huang et al.
papers.summary: Expert offloading enables Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained GPUs, but expert transfers and CPU execution limit decoding performance. Speculative decoding can mitigate these costs, yet separate draft weights consume scarce GPU memory and longer drafts increase verification demand. In this paper, we present CCAMoE, a unified runtime that coordinates adaptive speculative decoding with concurrent expert-cache updates. Its design has three key features: 1) Cache-only drafting, which reuses resident target experts to generate proposals and routing hints without separate draft weights; 2) Draft-guided cache updates, which anticipate expert demand and overlap transfers with computation to support subsequent drafting and verification; and 3) Cost-aware draft-length control, which balances expected acceptance against execution cost. Together, these mechanisms coordinate proposal generation and cache preparation through a shared evolving cache, improving proposal quality while reducing verification cost. Across various MoE models, GPU platforms, and workloads, CCAMoE consistently achieves the lowest decoding latency, with up to 2.33× speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Covertness Recovery in Multi-RAT UAV Swarms Under Post-Detection Threat Escalation via Lifelong Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Yinxuan Wu, Xiaohao Xia, Beatriz Lorenzo, Dennis Goeckel et al.
papers.summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms increasingly span multiple spectrum bands and radio access technologies (RATs), e.g., Wi-Fi, LoRa, Zigbee, and cellular. With active adversaries capable of protocol-aware jamming, spoofing, traffic analysis, and control-plane exploitation, survivable and timely covert communication is challenging. Moreover, after detection, adversaries may escalate with selective, adaptive attacks that increase latency and hinder recovery. This paper is the first to study covertness recovery under post-detection threat escalation. We design a learning-based mechanism that re-establishes covert communication across learning domains with different Willie densities and attack models, amid stochastic task arrivals, UAV mobility, and uncertain warden locations and behaviors. We jointly optimize RAT selection, resource allocation, and task offloading to minimize Age of Covert Information (AoCI), energy, and threat impact. Warden behavior is modeled via an adaptive attack-selection process capturing detection-triggered escalation and nonstationary strategies. We propose Cross-Domain Factorized Adaptive Lifelong Learning with Proximal Policy Opti- mization (CDFALL-PPO), which factorizes shared and domain-specific policy components for online adaptation while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Across three escalating 30-task sequences, extensive simulations show that CDFALL-PPO raises median packet covert delivery rate (PCR) by 14.5 %, increases covert throughput by up to 53.6%, and lowers AoCI by 59.4% relative to PPO. Under the strongest composite attack, mean on-attack PCR improves from 52% to 70%, and mean post-attack recovery PCR rises from 64% to 93%.

papers.title: ImCDN: An Immersive Content Delivery Network for Cooperative Tile-level 360 Video Streaming
papers.authors: Ning Wang, Xiaofan Liu, Beatriz Lorenzo, Sumudu Samarakoon
papers.summary: Delivering immersive 360 video over Content Distribution Networks (CDNs) demands ultra-high bitrates, yet each user's viewport covers only a small fraction of the full panorama. Therefore, conventional segment-level architectures waste scarce edge resources on unseen regions. This paper presents ImCDN, an immersive end-to-end tile-granularity CDN framework that integrates field-of-view (FoV)-driven cloud pre-distribution with hybrid segment-tile caching at edge servers, edge compute for on-demand tile transcoding, and an edge-to-edge relay mechanism for cooperative content sharing. We formulate the CDN optimization problem, comprising cache admission, compute scheduling, and serving-node selection, as a long-term utility maximization that balances cache hit-rate, edge sharing, end-to-end latency, backhaul traffic, energy consumption, viewport video quality, and cache replacement cost. We solve it via multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) under centralized training and decentralized execution across edge servers. Simulations on a realistic topology with real 360 head-tracking traces show that ImCDN improves edge hit rate and reduces user waiting time, reduces origin traffic by approximately 18% compared to the non-cooperative edge variant, and outperforms segment-only CDN baselines at comparable immersive quality (e.g., 4K/6K) and standard caching heuristics.

papers.title: Automated Safety Analysis for Agentic Workflows
papers.authors: Yanju Chen, Ying Li, Bosi Zhang, Hanzhi Liu et al.
papers.summary: LLM applications are increasingly built as agentic workflows: programs that combine model calls, external tools, and control logic to act autonomously on a user's behalf. Because these workflows execute real-world actions, logical flaws in how a workflow is wired can cause severe harm in deployed systems. Unlike prompt injections or malformed API calls, these workflow bugs stem from defects in the workflow's design, yet no existing tool can statically validate workflow logic across frameworks prior to deployment. We present Apsis, a static safety analyzer that detects workflow bugs before deployment. To operate across frameworks, Apsis lifts framework-specific code into a common intermediate representation (IR). This IR models a workflow as a semantic graph of steps, data dependencies, and shared state, while annotating each component with behavioral properties such as whether an input is mandatory or how a shared channel merges concurrent writes. Building on this representation, we introduce a bug description language that formalizes recurring classes of agentic failures as declarative patterns over the IR. By matching these patterns against the IR, Apsis detects structural and behavioral flaws and pinpoints the exact step responsible for each bug. To evaluate Apsis, we construct, to our knowledge, the first corpus of workflow bugs, distilled from real-world reports across 13 widely used frameworks. On a reproducible benchmark suite drawn from this corpus, Apsis detects workflow bugs with 91% precision and 84% recall, and uncovers 36 previously unknown bugs in real-world workflows.

papers.title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
papers.authors: Yixin Fang, Weili He
papers.summary: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.

papers.title: Diversity over Scale: Recursive Self-Improvement with Ensembles of Small Open-Weight Models
papers.authors: Navapat Nananukul, Mayank Kejriwal
papers.summary: The advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents across various tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) loops, in which a language model repeatedly rewrites a program and builds on its previous version, now perform well in machine-learning tasks, but they rely on frontier models and hundreds of calls per run. Small open-weight models are far cheaper, yet when used alone, their programs often crash and their improvements stall. We propose DiVE (diverse models evolve), an ensemble method for RSI that aims to improve creativity and diversity of generated solutions. DiVE uses three components: a shared memory, a failure log, and best-idea-wins rounds. This allows models to write candidate solutions from the same context and retain the best idea at each iteration. On 22 MLE-bench Lite competitions, an ensemble of five 8-12B open-weight models has 25.4% less test error than its average member and 16.7% less than Llama 3.3 70B, and comes within 7.1% of Qwen 3.5 122B-A10B at 75% of its cost. Diversity among small models can thus stand in for part of the scale that RSI relies on.

papers.title: Center-Aware Ordinal Learning for Prostate Cancer Grading from Histopathology Images
papers.authors: Mohammad Mahdi Abootorabi, Parvin Mousavi, Purang Abolmaesumi
papers.summary: Prostate cancer grading from histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) is complicated by the ordered nature of ISUP grades, class imbalance, and center-dependent variations in staining, tissue preparation, and scanning. Most weakly supervised methods treat grade groups as independent categories and may therefore learn representations that do not transfer reliably across institutions. We propose a center-aware ordinal learning framework that combines a pretrained pathology encoder with attention-based multiple instance learning. The framework uses an Earth Mover's Distance loss to account for ordinal errors, an ordinal supervised contrastive objective to align same-grade slides across centers while separating grades according to disease severity, and curriculum learning to reduce the dominance of benign cases. We evaluate the framework on approximately 9,100 biopsy WSIs from the two-center PANDA dataset. The proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 0.842 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.958 on the held-out test set. Its main benefit is observed in cross-center transfer: when a linear probe is trained on Karolinska representations and evaluated on Radboud, accuracy increases from 0.643 to 0.823 and quadratic weighted kappa from 0.899 to 0.930. Performance remains stable in the reverse direction. UMAP projections further show improved mixing between centers while preserving an ordinal grade trajectory. These results suggest that combining ordinal and center-aware objectives produces more transferable slide representations for multi-center prostate cancer grading.

papers.title: WingBench: Benchmarking How AI Agents Search for Better Designs
papers.authors: Yiming Yang, David Xia, Jisen Li, Yuqing Jian et al.
papers.summary: Design search often uses cheap learned predictions to choose which candidates deserve expensive tests, but these tests can fail, especially on the unusual designs that optimization favors. We introduce WingBench, a multifidelity benchmark in which optimizers and AI agents design transonic wings with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) inside the search. They can query a learned aerodynamic surrogate and spend a fixed budget of sequential CFD evaluations, each returning a score or a failure type. WingBench grades the design each method recommends, reporting separately whether it receives a valid score and how good that score is. Using WingBench, we contribute a study of five baseline optimizers and a comparison of three AI agent methods, which produced 6,629 CFD evaluation records. Feedback helps baseline optimizers deliver valid designs when it changes their later proposals, but the differential-evolution variant does so with lower aerodynamic quality. An open-ended research agent finds designs of similar quality to the strongest baselines over 32 CFD queries, with different prior information and unmatched total computation. In early search, our reflection and planning implementations do not consistently improve on it. We release the data, code, agent prompts, and analysis scripts for reproducibility.

papers.title: Belief-Driven Quantum Magnetometer Control for GPS-Denied Navigation
papers.authors: Murtuza Lemonwala, Laxima Niure Kandel
papers.summary: Autonomous vehicles increasingly need to navigate without satellite positioning. Magnetic anomaly navigation (Mag-Nav) with quantum magnetometers offers a passive, unjammable fix, but the low size-weight-and-power (SWaP) sensors that small drones can carry are weak, and they are operated open loop at a fixed setting. Interferometric (Ramsey) magnetometers face a trade-off: long interrogation times are more sensitive but become ambiguous when the expected field is uncertain. The navigator's own position belief, pushed through the anomaly map, predicts that field. We close this loop. The filter's predictive field distribution sets the Ramsey phase and interrogation time at every epoch, through a closed-form rule that moves between an ambiguity limit and a decoherence limit. We evaluate it on real U.S. Air Force flight data (real tracks, inertial drift, measured fields, and a survey map tested 18 months after it was flown), with only the Ramsey sensor modelled. Against fixed-setting baselines, 63 of 72 independent flight windows favour belief driven sensing (p = 2 × 10⁻¹¹). Error falls by 20-27% for low-SNR sensors and 30-44% for mid-contrast sensors. An ablation separates the two ingredients. Phase alignment drives the gain in steady flight, and the rule matches the best fixed setting without the hindsight tuning that setting requires. After a lost start, interrogation time adaptation is essential, cutting median error by 37-42% even against hindsight-tuned phase-aligned settings. Gains are small for high-quality sensors with accurate maps. On an IBM superconducting qubit, the rule's interrogation time stays within 1.3× of the empirical optimum. Coupled with information-aware routing, belief-driven sensing lowers mission error by 15-40%.

papers.title: ScaleEvals: Scaling Generalist Policy Evaluation through Reset-Free Autonomous Play
papers.authors: Amitoj Sandhu, Ethan Sick, Omkaar Buddhikot, Nadia Laswi et al.
papers.summary: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is bottlenecked by manual resets, human grading, and small fixed task suites with limited diagnostic coverage. We present ScaleEvals, a scalable reset-free protocol that evaluates policies through continuous physical play across a robot fleet. A VLM AutoPrompter generates scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags, enabling performance analysis across diverse rollouts. A VLM AutoGrader assesses task progress, achieving 90.7% agreement with human graders. Scores are aggregated via a soft-win Bradley-Terry model, while tag-stratified ANOVA provides interpretable capability diagnostics. Across 3,000+ physical autonomous rollouts on DROID and YAM, ScaleEvals achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hr per station while reducing active human labor by 98%. By ranking five SOTA generalist policies, ScaleEvals correlates with held-out manual evaluation ranking on DROID (r=0.94, rho=0.90, p=0.018), and remains internally consistent on a second embodiment, YAM (r=0.839, rho=0.80). Beyond aggregate rankings, we observe behavioral compositionality: recombining verb-, skill-, and object-conditioned evidence predicts policy order on unseen prompts. Across 10 tasks and 240 prospective physical rollouts, we recover three-policy orderings of 96% pairwise concordance, demonstrating ScaleEvals can predict not just which policy leads, but where rankings reverse.

papers.title: The Effect of Security-Focused Prompts on Reported Findings: A Controlled Experiment on 400 AI-Generated Web Applications
papers.authors: Darko Andročec
papers.summary: Agentic coding tools turn a specification into a running web application, so their defaults for authentication, sessions, input validation, and dependencies become its security posture. This study asks whether appending a fixed block of OWASP-aligned security requirements to the prompt changes what such tools produce, by how much, and with what side effects. Each of 100 frozen specifications was realized four times: two agentic tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI) crossed with two prompts sharing a byte-identical functional core, without (A) and with (B) the security block. A fixed static and dynamic pipeline scanned the 400 applications, yielding 6,721 triaged findings, analyzed with count and logistic mixed models and with a dependency diff. The block cut findings per application by a third (incidence-rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.60-0.71), equally through both tools, and roughly doubled the declared dependency surface, so variant-B applications carried more high-severity dependency advisories. Adjusted for that surface the advisory rate did not rise (flat per application, 18% lower in aggregate), while high-severity findings in first-party source fell by nearly half. Security-focused prompting is therefore an inexpensive and portable improvement, but it enlarges the dependency surface that has to be audited against it, an effect of library selection rather than of the security requirements themselves.

papers.title: Occupancy Planar Patch: Incremental Probabilistic Bounded-Plane Reconstruction from LiDAR Data
papers.authors: Jiahao Wang, Chaehyeon Song, Dongjiao He, Jan Quenzel et al.
papers.summary: Online surface reconstruction from LiDAR scans requires observation models that respect the sensor's physical measurement geometry. Unlike unordered point sets, LiDAR returns carry anisotropic range noise along known rays, which also implicitly identify free space. We introduce the Occupancy Planar Patch (OPP), an incremental bounded planar patch representation that evaluates surface likelihoods and free space directly in range-space, allowing sensor noise, plane uncertainty, and ray clearance to be explicitly modelled during reconstruction. A single ray-to-patch association weight jointly updates plane geometry, refines surface boundaries, and blends camera imagery. The method is evaluated using six sequences from the Oxford Spires and Multi-Campus datasets. OPP achieves the highest precision and lowest reconstruction error among evaluated methods, while producing stored maps among the most compact. By conservatively admitting surfaces only where geometric evidence is certain, OPP prioritises structural precision over unconstrained completeness, which is well suited for architectural modelling. Geometric reconstruction operates in real time, requiring 81 ms per frame on a representative sequence, with texture projection adding 134 ms.

papers.title: Plan Big, Paint Small: Semantic-Aware Computation Allocation for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.authors: Yixuan Luo, Yanjing Li
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion streams a video chunk by chunk, but large AR models are too slow for real-time use. We ask where in an AR rollout a large model is actually needed. Pairing Krea-Realtime-14B with Self-Forcing-1.3B, which share their latent space and denoising schedule, we find that the order of the two models matters: when the 14B model generates only the first chunk and the 1.3B model continues, the rollout keeps 95% of the 14B model's semantic advantage, whereas the reverse allocation keeps 16% at about ten times the cost.
