In this paper we: i) prove that, for flow matching and diffusion ODEs, BayesDiff's total variance decays at rate O(1/T) as the number of Euler steps T used by the solver increases; ii) introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), two recursions inspired by the extended and unscented Kalman filters that fix this problem by carrying the cross-covariance between state and weights; and iii) widen the last-layer posterior with observation embeddings the policy already computes, improving uncertainty estimates without retraining for CoMP and several test-time estimators alike. We demonstrate these benefits on three manipulation benchmarks with applications in failure detection and demonstration selection for fine-tuning, where CoMP corrects BayesDiff's variance collapse while matching or outperforming several uncertainty estimators.

papers.title: LoCo-WAM: Test-Time Training as Long Context for World-Action Models
papers.authors: Sheng Cheng, Deqian Kong
papers.summary: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.

papers.title: How Far Can LLMs Go in Generating Android Lint Checks from Natural Language?
papers.authors: Moshood A. Fakorede, A. B. Siddique, Manu Sridharan, Umar Farooq
papers.summary: Static analysis tools such as Android Lint, PMD, and CodeQL let developers add custom checks for project-specific rules. However, authoring a check is a demanding programming task: a rule can be stated in a few sentences, yet turning it into a working, tested check requires detailed knowledge of the analysis framework and its issue-detection logic. Recent work generates such checks with large language models (LLMs), but each system needs more than the natural language description a developer always has: a bug-fix patch, a CVE record, or a developer-written test suite to repair against. No prior work measures whether an LLM can turn a description into a working check, or what external knowledge it needs to do so. We introduce LintBench, a human-validated benchmark of 113 real-world Android Lint checks, each paired with a natural language description and its original test suite as a held-out oracle. We evaluate four LLMs, including proprietary and open-weight models. We compare prompting strategies, then evaluate execution-guided repair with and without retrieved API knowledge. Prompting alone reaches 30%-65% (pass@5) across models. Execution-guided repair and retrieval reach 57%-85% test-passing rates within five calls. Our results show that execution feedback raises the pass rate, while retrieved framework knowledge raises the compile rate, which reaches up to 99%. The framework knowledge helps the low-performing models the most, providing the knowledge they need to fix compilation errors. Of the generated checks that compile but fail their tests, 87% have false negatives, missing an issue the generated check should report. Based on our findings, getting the issue-detection logic right remains an open challenge. We release LintBench and the evaluation harness to support future work on generating Android Lint checks.

papers.title: AROMA: Understanding AI Support For Mental Well-being through Role Theory
papers.authors: Issac Ting, Ethan Pan, Koustuv Saha, Hua Shen et al.
papers.summary: AI supporters for mental well-being are becoming more prevalent. When these AI supporters start acting in ways beyond their expected function it leads to relational harm. Standard approaches to evaluating such AI supporters are limited to inspecting their efficacy in narrow task-specific settings, which do not explain these discrepancies in expected and actual behavior. To address this gap, we propose the AROMA (A Role-Oriented Model of Analysis) framework to provide a common role taxonomy for different support contexts. We developed AROMA using a theory-informed annotation of over 7,515 conversations from 13 datasets and propose eight "Role States" based on observed-not prescribed-behavior. We show these Role States vary according to the context of support; depict unique structural and temporal characteristics of AI supporters vis-a-vis Humans; and inform novel AI support prompting strategy for better role alignment. This framework provides a new lens to understand AI support failures.

papers.title: Contention-Aware Flexible Execution for Machine Learning Workloads
papers.authors: Marco Kurzynski, Shaizeen Aga, Di Wu
papers.summary: Concurrent kernel execution is a ubiquitous paradigm in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) across both training and inference. That said, concurrency causes potential slowdown as concurrent kernels contend for limited GPU resources (cores, caches, memory bandwidth), which are shared between these kernels rather than exclusively available to one, as in isolated execution. This raises an important research question: to what extent does concurrency slow down kernel execution and how can it be mitigated. To answer this question, our work presents two studies. First, we characterize concurrent kernel execution extensively for the first time, to our knowledge. We conduct not just performance analysis of concurrent kernels but also memory behavior under concurrency on state-of-the-art AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs designed for datacenter AI, using the AMD-internal millisecond sampler. Based on the observations, we share insights on the slowdown along two dimensions (memory vs. compute bound, large vs. small kernels) to inform future optimizations. Second, we put the derived insights to use, aiming to deliver higher performance via targeted, flexible overlap of ML operators. Frameworks today make the simple decision of early-first for concurrent kernels, which is suboptimal. Noticing the opportunity that ML dataflow has inherent flexibility in which operators can be overlapped and how hardware resources can be allocated, we deduce simple heuristics to tune both overlap anchors and resource allocation for concurrent kernels to improve performance. We evaluate our proposed contention-aware flexible execution (termed CAFEML) across a variety of ML scenarios (inference decode, inference prefill, training) and demonstrate a speedup of up to 13% end-to-end with simple scheduling changes and no kernel rewrites.

papers.title: Explain Your Code: AI-Based Examination at Class Scale
papers.authors: David Sarne, Shachar Sagi, Yossi Ben-Zion
papers.summary: Generative AI has weakened the link between working code and a student's understanding of it. Oral examination, the traditional test of that understanding, does not scale to large courses. We report the full-course deployment of a three-agent AI system that examines students on their own code. The first, the examiner, asks three questions anchored to specific lines of the submission, adapting difficulty to each answer, in a 16-minute text dialogue. The other two grade: a code reviewer that never sees the examination and a grader without direct access to the code. Authorship is assessed separately and is advisory. The system examined 247 students in an operating systems course (three exercises, 546 sittings, two examination languages). The grader's oral score was uncorrelated with the same submission's code quality score (Spearman rho = -0.073, 95% CI [-0.205, 0.063], n = 216) yet tracked degree grade point average (rho = 0.419, [0.294, 0.523], n = 214), while automated test scores sat at the ceiling. The mean of a student's two oral scores correlated with grade point average at 0.468 ([0.353, 0.568], n = 210), within the range of grades in three single-semester courses built on programming assignments. Model spend averaged at most 1.37 per sitting. In surveys, students began skeptical of the AI examination and rated it more favorably after sitting it twice. These results indicate that examining students on their own code is feasible at class scale, and that its score relates to academic standing where the code quality score does not.

papers.title: Impact of Edge Software Evolution on Audio Tagging Models: An Empirical Study on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano
papers.authors: Guillem Fustier-Castillo, Ruben Ribes-Serrano, Jordi Grau-Haro, Marta Garcia-Ballesteros et al.
papers.summary: Audio tagging is a fundamental task in machine listening, enabling the automatic identification of acoustic events in applications such as intelligent monitoring, industrial inspection, environmental sensing, and smart environments. As these applications increasingly migrate to edge platforms, deployment-oriented metrics such as latency, energy consumption, and resource utilization become critical alongside predictive performance. However, most existing studies evaluate audio tagging models under a single software environment, overlooking the potential impact of software stack evolution on deployment efficiency. This paper investigates how software ecosystem updates affect the execution characteristics of state-of-the-art audio tagging architectures on edge devices. We evaluate representative convolutional and Transformer-based models, including PANNs (CNN and ResNet variants), AST, and PaSST, on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano platform using two generations of NVIDIA's software ecosystem: JetPack 6.2 and JetPack 7.2. Under identical hardware conditions, we analyze inference latency, energy consumption, CPU/GPU utilization, and memory footprint across multiple inference backends and power modes. The results show that software stack evolution can substantially affect deployment performance. JetPack 7.2 reduces latency and energy consumption by more than 50% for several convolutional architectures when combined with TensorRT, while significantly increasing GPU utilization. In contrast, AST exhibits only marginal gains, whereas PaSST shows intermediate behavior. These findings demonstrate that software evolution is a critical factor in Edge AI evaluation and can alter the relative deployment efficiency of competing architectures. Consequently, software stack versions should be explicitly considered when benchmarking and selecting audio tagging models for embedded deployment.

papers.title: Skill-JEPA: Learning Planner-Aligned Action Spaces for World Models
papers.authors: Tomás Couso Coddou, Christ Devia, Rex G. Liu, Rodrigo Toro Icarte
papers.summary: World models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn from pixels to predict the outcome of actions in a latent space. To reach a goal, a planner samples many candidate action sequences, uses the model to predict where each one leads, and executes the best one. However, standard planners draw their candidates from a Gaussian, while the model has only seen the structured, state-dependent actions of its training data. Its predictions for such candidates are unreliable, and planning fails more often as goals move farther away. We propose Skill-JEPA, which learns an action space aligned with the planner. A variational autoencoder conditioned on the current state encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a standard Gaussian prior, and decodes them back into actions. The world model predicts the effect of skills rather than raw actions, and the planner searches over skills starting from that same Gaussian, so its candidates resemble the model's training data. Skill-JEPA adds a single module, trained end-to-end with the world model, and leaves the planner untouched, with no subgoals, hierarchy, or hand-designed skills. Across three JEPA world models and four benchmarks, average success on goals 80 steps away rises from 42% with raw actions to 62%; the gains grow with goal distance and hold across four planners. On AntMaze, a quadruped locomotion task, success on goals two maze cells away rises from 0.4% to 38%. This suggests that part of the difficulty of reaching distant goals lies in the action space, and can be removed without changing the planner.

papers.title: A Unified Framework for Intelligent Cyber Attack Detection and Alert Correlation
papers.authors: Miguel Silva, João Vitorino, Daniela Pinto, Eva Maia et al.
papers.summary: A Security Operations Center (SOC) plays a critical role in detecting, correlating, and responding to modern cyber threats. However, SOCs continue to face challenges related to alert overload, fragmented detection capabilities, and limited collaboration between analysts and automated systems. These issues often result in delayed incident response, analyst fatigue, and an increased risk of overlooking sophisticated, multi-stage attacks that unfold gradually across different layers of the network. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a unified framework for network traffic classification and alert correlation through the use of signature rules, machine learning, and sequential pattern mining algorithms. The solution was evaluated in a controlled testbed environment emulating realistic, multi-stage attack scenarios, including malware exploitation, lateral movement, reconnaissance, and data exfiltration. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in detecting and correlating complex attack behaviors, while providing analysts with actionable insights in line with a human-in-the-loop approach to SOC operations.

papers.title: Acoustic Markers of Engagement in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Their Caregivers
papers.authors: Young Suh Hong, Kaleen Shrestha, Austin Joel Dympep, Maja Matarić
papers.summary: Characterizing user engagement is essential for developing effective human-computer interaction (HCI) applications, particularly for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Because home-based HCI naturally involves caregivers as conversational facilitators, analyzing both child and caregiver vocalizations can provide critical insights into characterizing interaction dynamics. Using a dataset of home-based socially assistive robot (SAR) interventions, this work demonstrates how child and caregiver vocalization patterns can model engagement in HCI contexts. We employed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) with child and caregiver acoustic data to identify acoustic features that significantly differentiated engagement from disengagement. The results demonstrated that children and caregivers share three significant acoustic markers of engagement: mean Alpha Ratio (AlphaRatio), mean Harmonics-to-Noise Ratio (HNR), and mean Spectral Slope 500-1500 (SlopeV500-1500). This reflects cleaner and smoother vocalizations during engagement across both groups. Furthermore, we evaluated a State x Group interaction model to compare the magnitudes of standardized state-dependent differences between children and caregivers. The results indicated that children exhibit significantly greater state-related variation than caregivers in three acoustic features: AlphaRatio, HNR, and SlopeV500-1500.

papers.title: NitroGen: Observations on the Action Dynamics, Visual Instruction Following, and Spatial Exploration
papers.authors: Shengyuan Lin, Zhiling Li, Haoyu Nie, Ozan K. Tonguz
papers.summary: NitroGen is an open vision-action foundation model for game control. It is trained by behavior cloning on online gameplay videos. In this paper, we study the frozen controller in Hollow Knight and Trackmania as examples along three dimensions: action adaptation, visual instruction following, and spatial exploration. Our results indicate that NitroGen can adapt its actions to local context, but it lacks the planning, recovery, and exploration needed for longer-horizon game control.

papers.title: Trajectories Through Parsons Problems: Making Student Difficulty Patterns Visible to Instructors
papers.authors: Daniel Prol, Juho Leinonen, Arto Hellas, Saleh Alkhamees et al.
papers.summary: Existing Parsons problem tools primarily focus on correctness, indicating whether a student solved a problem, but providing limited visibility into the underlying problem-solving process. Without that visibility, instructors cannot see which blocks caused repeated confusion or which distractors were consistently selected. We introduce Pulla, a Parsons problem tool that instruments programming assignments to capture fine-grained interaction data. We examine what these behavioral traces make visible to instructors, namely how long students take on a problem and how many moves they make, which recurring errors the distractors expose and how the class arrives at them, whether those errors follow a student from one problem to the next, and which students complete the whole assignment without a single error.

papers.title: Efficient Conversational Multi-Talker ASR with Predicted Speaker-Agnostic Activity Streams
papers.authors: Xiluo He, Magdalena Rybicka, Laureano Moro-Velazquez, Jesús Villalba et al.
papers.summary: Multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR) can be performed by conditioning a single-speaker recognizer on frame-level speaker activity. However, this approach requires a complete diarization pass to obtain the conditioning signals and one ASR pass per speaker, making both the frontend and recognition costs dependent on the number of speakers. We reduce these costs by using Heuristic Error Assignment Training (HEAT) to merge the activities of an arbitrary number of speakers into two speaker-agnostic streams. Conditioning on these streams limits recognition to two ASR passes regardless of the number of participants. Through an analysis of the resulting encoder representations, we show that under a stream-assignment heuristic suited to conversational speech, the recognizer represents a stream target much as it does a speaker target. Because the streams do not encode persistent speaker identities, we further replace the conventional sliding-window diarization and clustering frontend with a model that predicts both activity streams directly from the audio in a single pass. A combination of arrival-order and permutation-invariant training objectives over the two-stream powerset labels prevents the predictor from collapsing to identical streams. We also investigate post-hoc speaker attribution by matching decoded utterances to speaker activities within their assigned streams. Experiments on corpora with diverse conversational dynamics demonstrate a favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoff. On AMI and ICSI, two-stream conditioning is respectively 44% and 87% faster than per-speaker conditioning using the same diarization frontend, with less than 2% relative WER degradation. Direct activity prediction increases these speedups to 79% and 132%, with relative WER degradations of 10% and 21%, respectively.

papers.title: CADENCE:Temporally Coherent Whole-Body Human Mesh Recovery that Preserves Expressive Hand Motion
papers.authors: Keniel Peart, Jagmohan Chauhan, Indu P. Bodala, Shelly Vishwakarma
papers.summary: Whole-body SMPL-X estimators recover body, hand, and face meshes from single images, but applied frame by frame to video they produce jittery motion. Smoothing the output removes the jitter at a cost that body-only benchmarks do not measure: a temporal filter strong enough to steady the torso also flattens the fast finger strokes that carry meaning in sign language and gesture. We present CADENCE, a whole-body SMPL-X system for monocular video designed around this trade-off. A per-frame estimator built on a shared C-RADIOv4 encoder, with a high-resolution hand pathway that reuses the same encoder on hand crops, produces each frame's estimate. An offline temporal refiner then filters the SMPL-X rotation sequence: attention along the kinematic tree selects, for every joint and every frame, a mixture of learned zero-phase filters, so the torso is smoothed while fast finger strokes pass through. On 3DPW, the refiner reduces acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2 while lowering PA-MPJPE from 41.9 to 40.2 mm; generic smoothers applied to the same predictions reach 6.2 to 7.7 mm/s2. On SignAvatars/How2Sign sign-language sequences, the refiner has the lowest hand jitter among the compared smoothers while keeping a hand-speed peak amplitude of 0.98, against 0.35 for a SmoothNet retrained on the full SMPL-X vector. The per-frame estimator also obtains the lowest full-body mesh error (25.7 mm) and hand joint error (8.3 mm) among the compared methods on EHF.

papers.title: FACET: A Data-Efficient Regional Parametric Head Model
papers.authors: Mathieu Lamarre, Elly Akhoundi, Thibault Goyallon, Patrick Anderson et al.
papers.summary: Production face pipelines need parametric head models that are expressive, FACS-controllable, and buildable on a small, fixed pool of identities. More training identities would always help, but high-quality registered head scans are expensive to capture; when scaling the data is not an option, the remaining lever is architecture. We present FACET, a parametric head model that makes the most of a fixed identity pool through architectural locality rather than more scans, and makes three contributions, each isolated against a matched global-PCA ablation on our own topology, training set, and normalization. (1) A regional identity decomposition into 16 anatomical regions bypasses the N-1 rank ceiling of a global PCA, driving held-out neutral-fit error from a 1.95 mm floor down to 0.23 mm on the same training identities. (2) A learned FACS action-unit expression model with per-identity neural personalization not only stays FACS-controllable but beats a properly-regularized global expression PCA at every component count – refuting the argument that FACS is too overcomplete to fit. (3) A dedicated neck/shoulder region reduces pose leakage into the pose-invariant upper face during unposing. Together, these show that architectural locality is the effective lever for a production head model under a fixed identity budget.

papers.title: TacHOI: Contact-Aware Object Reconstruction and Tracking for Egocentric Videos
papers.authors: Jackson Codd, Haoyu Li, Xianyi Cheng
papers.summary: Egocentric videos offer a scalable source of human demonstrations for robot learning. However, recovering metric object geometry and motion from monocular video is hindered by scale-depth ambiguity and hand-induced occlusion, while image-derived contact and shape priors alone cannot uniquely determine metric scale. We introduce TacHOI, a training-free framework that integrates tactile contact with monocular vision for joint hand-object reconstruction and tracking, without requiring object templates or depth sensors. Starting from pretrained visual estimates, TacHOI uses tactile contact to constrain object depth relative to the estimated hand, while spatially separated contacts on a metrically calibrated hand provide a physical ruler for object extent. It incorporates these constraints into a joint optimization of hand poses, object trajectories, and anisotropic object scale alongside visual alignment. Across 100 ARCTIC and HO3D sequences with synthesized tactile observations, TacHOI achieves the lowest median ADD-S* among the evaluated baselines, reducing error from 15.6 to 3.6 cm on ARCTIC and achieving 2.8 cm on HO3D. Additional experiments on OpenTouch demonstrate its applicability to measured tactile observations.

papers.title: Windchime: an Audiovisual Installation with Audio-Language Model implementations
papers.authors: Trent Eriksen, Celeste Betancur Gutierrez
papers.summary: Windchime is an audiovisual installation in which spoken language retrieves music and interactive animations from an artist authored corpus. A local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model transcribes each prompt while an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape with live coded Strudel fragments that layer into audio output. Simultaneously each spoken input results in retrieval of interactive Three.js animation scenes each containing unique tactile control via monome grid and arc hardware. Windchime distributes agency in three distinct directions; across the artist who authored the possible outputs, the ALM that influences what areas of the corpus can be retrieved, and the visitor whose spoken inputs result in multimodal embodied interaction.

papers.title: Bird-Call Recognition Across Distance: Acoustic Degradation and BirdNET Performance
papers.authors: Hasmik Gharibyan, Bhaskar Krishnamachari
papers.summary: As bird calls weaken with distance, their recordings lose spectral detail. We examine how species recognition varies with distance using controlled playback of ten-second excerpts from 20 bird species at seven distances from 1 to 48 ft. An STM32-based recording system acquires and stores the audio, which is subsequently analyzed on a computer using acoustic measurements and BirdNET. Across four metadata configurations, mean-aggregated top-1 accuracy is 95–100% through 24 ft, 90–95% at 36 ft, and 80–90% at 48 ft, with 20 recordings evaluated per configuration at each distance. Across the screened recordings, the median upper spectral edge is below its 1-ft reference at every evaluated distance from 4 to 36 ft, indicating an overall reduction in upper-frequency content with distance. These results show that recognition remains high through 24 ft despite measurable spectral degradation, followed by greater and configuration-dependent losses at longer distances.

papers.title: Exploring Early Vulnerability Analysis via Automatic Identification of Vulnerability-Introducing Commits
papers.authors: Weiliang Qi, Shu Wang, Youpeng Li, Ela Guo et al.
papers.summary: Developing effective vulnerability analysis techniques requires high-quality datasets that capture how vulnerabilities appear and evolve in real software codebase. Existing datasets, however, typically label as vulnerable only the code immediately preceding vulnerability-fixing commits (VFCs), overlooking the earlier versions in which vulnerabilities were first introduced and subsequently evolved. This practice limits both dataset coverage and our understanding of whether current detectors can identify vulnerabilities during their early, latent stages. In this paper, we present three manually annotated datasets of vulnerability-introducing commits (VICs) based on recent CVEs and widely used open-source projects. We further propose D-SZZ, a data state-aware VIC identification framework that analyzes security-fixing patterns and performs vulnerability scope slicing to recover the semantics implied by a fix. Experimental results demonstrate that D-SZZ outperforms existing SZZ and LLM-based baselines in identifying VICs. In addition, we evaluate six representative vulnerability detectors and find that models trained only on pre-VFC code struggle with original vulnerabilities, while incorporating early-stage samples improves detection performance. We also show that D-SZZ improves downstream vulnerable-version identification, and use it to uncover 16 inaccurate affected-version records in the NVD, all of which were officially confirmed and updated.

papers.title: From Observation to Explanation: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM-Generated Code for Principled Repair
papers.authors: Musfiqur Rahman
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development, yet our understanding of how they generate code remains critically underdeveloped. We address this gap by triangulating evidence across three layers. Longitudinally, autonomous agent-attributed code is statistically indistinguishable from human code under a semantic modification definition (HR = 1.019, p = 0.490), yet attracts disproportionately corrective modifications in production (49.1% vs 37.9% human baseline). This finding demands a causal explanation. Empirically, existing benchmarks overestimate LLM capabilities: models that achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks attain only 24 to 35% on real-world class-level code. Behaviourally, detection systems reveal puzzling asymmetries: GPT-3.5 is far more detectable than modern models (AUC-ROC = 0.96, a 27-point gap), even though modern models produce mutually similar code structures; yet no single feature reliably distinguishes AI-generated from human code at the class level, and the leading commercial detector achieves only 15 to 64% recall. Together, these findings raise a question that empirical studies cannot answer: why do LLMs generate code with these properties? This thesis proposes mechanistic interpretability, a causal token-level circuit tracing, as the bridge between empirical observation and principled correction. By identifying the transformer circuits responsible for detectable stylistic signatures, hallucination patterns, and systematic defects, we aim to drive an agentic repair framework that intervenes at the causal source of defects rather than patching surface symptoms.

papers.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
papers.authors: Jinbin Luo, Xiaozhe Yao, Shang Yang, Zhijian Liu et al.
papers.summary: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU–GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20–59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40–3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

papers.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
papers.authors: Amine Lbath, Manan Suri, Aurelien Delaitre, Vadim Okun et al.
papers.summary: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Complementarity-Based Contact Models for Robotics
papers.authors: Onur Beker, A. René Geist, Michael Posa, Marc Toussaint et al.
papers.summary: Simulating rigid-body dynamics with contact is fundamental to robotics, from motion synthesis and control to mechanism design. Many widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, whose physical assumptions and numerical solution require substantial background. While excellent surveys, monographs, and course notes exist, they mostly address computational mechanics or computer graphics or document a single simulator. To the best of our knowledge, a self-contained pedagogical treatment for robotics, bringing these formulations and their solvers together with complete derivations and a unified notation, does not yet exist. This tutorial addresses this gap by connecting rigid-body dynamics, conic optimization, and frictional contact. In particular, we explain how complementarity conditions encode non-penetration and frictional dissipation, determining separation, sticking, and sliding without prescribed contact modes. We distinguish equivalent transcriptions from convex relaxations, showing how the latter can introduce artifacts such as lift-off and creep. We examine the existence and uniqueness of motion and contact forces, including the solver's role in selecting among multiple solutions. We then compare first-order and Newton-based methods, explain regularization and proximal strategies, and discuss trade-offs between computational cost, robustness, and physical fidelity. Connections to widely used simulators, optimal control, and differentiable simulation help readers interpret simulation results, choose suitable formulations and solvers, and develop their own contact dynamics routines.

papers.title: Verify the Verifier: Specification-Grounded LLM Cross-Checking for Bugs That Escape UVM Scoreboards
papers.authors: Ana E. Sanchez Villalobos, Michael D. Quinn, Aakash Tyagi, Minh D. Luu et al.
papers.summary: A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification, termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches. We present Verify the Verifier, to our knowledge the first framework whose LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker examines a passing regression's traces against the specification. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 are candidate scoreboard escapes: non-equivalent, exercised by the tests, yet passing. The framework confirmed 41 as scoreboard escapes with assertions failing on the buggy design and proven on the original.

papers.title: STEGOGUARD-LM: Evaluating End-to-End Protection Against LLM Covert Channels
papers.authors: Martha Dimgba, George Williams
papers.summary: A defense that disrupts hidden messages may still provide little protection if its detector rarely triggers an intervention. We present StegoGuard-LM, a controlled framework for evaluating defenses against covert messages in large language model outputs. We examine token-rank and synonym channels, with Unicode concealment as a structural control, and track messages through detection, intervention, and recovery. Deterministic rewriting prevented full recovery of 103 of 104 synonym-encoded messages when applied unconditionally, but only one when intervention depended on a detector set to limit false alarms. In a four-round replay on a 48-response subset, an attacker selecting from a fixed catalog recovered more bits by switching channels, although paired gains were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Randomized rewriting showed no sustained advantage in this pilot. A more sensitive detector improved protection but modified about one-third of clean responses. These findings show how uneven detection can undermine effective rewriting and why protection must be evaluated alongside attacker adaptation and intervention on legitimate text.

papers.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
papers.authors: Ziqing Yang, Yixin Wu, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
papers.summary: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1% and 81.6% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2% and 22.4% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

papers.title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
papers.authors: Sean Tang, Peiran Wang, Ying Li, Esha Shivakumar et al.
papers.summary: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

papers.title: Thinflow: Organizing HPC Benchmarking Campaigns as Rerunnable Directory Trees
papers.authors: Richard Schulze, Ari Rasch, Anna-Lena Roth, Jonas Posner
papers.summary: A benchmarking campaign provides the measurements behind an HPC performance study: code variants are built, swept over core or node counts, and measured repeatedly. Moving such a campaign to another supercomputer or rerunning it months later requires work that is not part of the study itself. Job scripts are adapted to each supercomputer, and what exactly ran is often reconstructed afterwards. We present Thinflow, a small Bash engine for organizing HPC benchmarking campaigns as rerunnable directory trees of tasks and runs. A task is a directory with a short shell script next to the code. For each sweep, one command builds the code, runs the benchmarks, and plots the results. Thinflow derives the execution order from declared dependencies and writes it to a plain-text manifest. Per-supercomputer profiles submit the runs to a workload manager such as Slurm. Each run writes a provenance record of its environment, hardware, and parameters. The engine ships inside the campaign directory, so a campaign stays rerunnable without installing a separate tool and, once completed, may serve as a paper artifact. In a case study, we ran one campaign with identical task files on three Slurm partitions of two supercomputers, on up to 16 nodes. This strong-scaling study of matrix multiplication in C/OpenMP, C/MPI, and Julia/MPI comprises 37 task files with 217 non-comment lines. Its 455 benchmark runs recorded what differed per partition, chiefly profiles and command-line parameters. This suggests that such a campaign needs little structure beyond plain shell files.

papers.title: Anticipating Future Build Results with BuildPredictor
papers.authors: Christian Macho, Katharina Stengg
papers.summary: Continuous Integration (CI) is a popular programming practice for the seamless integration of code changes into the code base. Using CI, developers benefit from automated assembling and testing of the code after each commit. However, while the frequent integration and building supports developers, it also comes at the high costs of wasting time and resources for minimal changes. In this work, we investigate the potential of reducing the drawbacks by anticipating the build outcome using machine learning techniques. In particular, we propose a random forest model with various features such as changes to the source and build code, and changes to the complexity of the code. We observe that our model shows a good performance in an intra-project and holistic setting yielding a median MCC of 0.82 and 0.86, respectively. We also found that the most important features of our model concern the historical build result information. Additionally, we investigated the development of the performance of our model over time and found that our model can quickly arrive at its peak performance. In an additional experiment, we removed the hard-to-interpret historical build information features and found that our model still yields decent performance while improving the interpretability of it. Summarizing, our model can help to avoid unnecessary build runs by anticipating the build result and thus, save resources.

papers.title: Introducing ReTiNA-Cinema: Real-Time Neuro-Augmented Cinema via Generative AI
papers.authors: Antoine Bellemare-Pepin, Philipp Thölke, Yann Harel, Mar Estarellas et al.
papers.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is currently revolutionizing content creation across various media. Between those who fear it will replace human creativity and those who regard it solely as a tool, many in the creative industries are beginning to view generative AI as a collaborator. Yet interaction with these systems often relies on discrete, turn-based prompting that can interrupt flow and constrain expression to symbolic text. We explore physiological signals as a source of continuous adaptation without explicit commands, as a path toward embodied co-creation. This paper presents ReTiNA-Cinema, a methodological proof-of-concept that integrates electroencephalography (EEG) with generative AI to enable physiologically guided visual modulation of cinematic material. By linking physiological activity to the evolving appearance of a film, the system provides a basis for exploring embodied sense-making, in which viewers' bodily responses contribute to shaping the sensory experience through which they interpret the unfolding scenes. The system combines real-time EEG signal processing with a generative AI pipeline based on Stable Diffusion Turbo for frame-level image transformation. Single-user and two-user configurations map EEG-derived features to prompt selection and transformation strength. ReTiNA-Cinema offers a framework for exploring how the physiology of viewers might influence a film's visual presentation, extending the possibilities for participation in cinematic experiences and storytelling. This system raises questions about the effects on engagement, perceived agency, and emotional response, which remain open to future empirical study. Video illustrations: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLMu36WzSQKiVeBnrUdwUAoUhqLqGX3bw and implementation: https://github.com/KairosHive/retina-cinema.

papers.title: StarMPI-SVD: Distributed-Memory Parallel Star-M Tensor SVD
papers.authors: Naman Pesricha, Grey Ballard, Srinivas Eswar, Md Taufique Hussain et al.
papers.summary: The star-M tensor algebra generalizes the optimal compression guarantees of the matrix singular value decomposition (SVD) to higher-order tensors. The t-SVDM-I decomposition is computed using a set of invertible transformations and slice-wise truncated SVDs with a prescribed rank, and its adaptive, multirank variant t-SVDM-II can determine slice-wise ranks to satisfy a prescribed error tolerance. Existing implementations of these algorithms are limited to shared-memory environments, restricting their applicability to modern large-scale datasets. In this work, we present the first distributed-memory implementations of t-SVDM-I and t-SVDM-II, which are generalized to N-way tensors. To address computational and communication bottlenecks, we design asynchronous, non-blocking communication strategies for efficient data redistribution to obtain highly efficient key computational kernels. Strong-scaling experiments demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of our approach (at least 70% parallel efficiency on up to 128 nodes, or 6144 cores), and we apply the star-M compression techniques to a set of application datasets of size up to 768 GB.

papers.title: Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue
papers.authors: Rishabh Ravi, Tony Hong, Chen Wang, Yue Zhu et al.
papers.summary: LLM agents run long, multi-turn programs whose contexts grow at every step, and serving them is limited by KV cache capacity. To alleviate this limitation, systems use context compression techniques, which typically wait until the KV cache crosses a large threshold and then summarize large spans of history at once, either in the background while the agent progresses or on the critical path. These summarizations can be done using the same model running on the same engine, or using the same or a different model running on extra hardware. When running on the same engine, summarization competes with the requests being served for both compute and memory capacity. To maximize the cost-effectiveness of summarization, this paper presents a new serving system called Aggron. Aggron summarizes agentic requests at every turn and selectively summarizes only certain parts of the KV cache. As a result, Aggron retains accuracy and keeps summarization requests lightweight. Moreover, Aggron launches summarization requests from a separate Summarization Queue while the corresponding agentic request whose KV cache we want to compress is stalled in the main request queue due to head-of-line stalls. The Summarization queue utilizes compute and memory capacity left over by the head-of-line stalls in the main queue. Further, to maximize efficiency, the server issues summarizations only when it predicts that they can complete before the corresponding agentic request will finally execute. In our evaluation, we compare Aggron to state-of-the-art asynchronous summarization. At high load, Aggron reduces P99 program latency by 27–31%, and raises throughput by 1.34–1.40×.

papers.title: FFGaussType: Feed-Forward Conversion of Glyph and SVG Geometry into Compact Gaussian Assets
papers.authors: Haoan Feng, Tianfu Wang, Peimeng Guan, Dae Yeol Lee et al.
papers.summary: Immersive 3D content allows text and graphical elements, such as subtitles, annotations, and icons, to be placed inside a scene rather than displayed as flat overlays. Placed this way, they respect occlusion and perspective and take on user-assigned materials and lighting while preserving their original shapes. In Gaussian scenes, however, each new glyph or icon requires its own iterative optimization, which limits scalable content creation. We present FFGaussType, which converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into Gaussian assets in a single forward pass. A point encoder maps anchors sampled on the known surface to a single feature plane, from which a decoder shared by all assets predicts neural Gaussians carrying surface normals. This separates geometric conversion from material and lighting choices, and the feature plane supports image and video coding for compact delivery. We construct a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with anchors and calibrated normal and silhouette renderings, holding out font families for evaluation. Conversion from prepared anchors takes 9.1 ms per asset, at a fraction of the compute and memory of prior baselines. On unseen font families and test icons, FFGaussType achieves 1.62° normal error and 0.985 silhouette IoU, the best among the compared feed-forward converters, matching the fidelity that per-asset fitting needs thousands of steps to reach. The code and dataset will be released after publication.

papers.title: Rethinking Utility in Differentially Private Visualization: A Channel-Centric Perspective
papers.authors: Jing Yang, Sarayu Pacca, Zhaocong Yang, Liyue Fan
papers.summary: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to protect sensitive data in visualization, but understanding how privacy-induced noise affects visual representations remains fragmented. Prior work has examined the impact of DP noise on specific chart types, yet these findings are typically tied to particular chart types and evaluation settings, making it difficult to generalize across contexts. In parallel, visualization research has long established that visual channels, the visual properties of marks that encode data attributes, differ in perceptual effectiveness under noise-free conditions. However, these principles have not been systematically revisited under DP, where noise is deliberately introduced into the data to protect privacy. In this paper, we present a channel-centric perspective to reframe prior empirical and theoretical results. Our synthesis drawson prior findings to motivate a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis: the utility of DP visualizations may depend on the task-relevant reads made salient by visual channel configurations and DP mechanism choice jointly. Moreover, this perspective highlights the role of channel choice throughout the privacy-preserving visualization pipeline, from disclosure framing and DP algorithm design to utility evaluation and interpretation of noisy outputs. The synthesis also identifies gaps in the existing evaluation literature and highlights research opportunities for channel-aware DP visualization.

papers.title: Static Analysis Guidance for Secure LLM Code Generation
papers.authors: Daniele Lunghi, Alberick Euraste Djiré, Zacharie Chenail-Larcher, Mélissa Tessa et al.
papers.summary: Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.

papers.title: SWE-Recreation: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Software Recreation
papers.authors: Zhiyao Xu, Zhanjie Ding, Hongyao Yu, Jingyu Xiao
papers.summary: Agents increasingly operate software and even write it, yet they are almost always told what to achieve: given a goal, a mock-up, or a demonstration. We ask whether an agent can instead understand an unfamiliar product by using it, and then rebuild it. The agent sees only rendered pixels and acts through pointer and keyboard, without access to the DOM, source, logs, or back-end. Within this interface, it explores, generates a replica, and checks its own work before evaluation. We present SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications (28 websites and 26 Android apps) with 1,446 hidden requirements describing multistep, stateful workflows and explicit exclusions for behavior outside the reconstruction scope. A fixed judge grades workflows with pixel evidence; a separate post-hoc judge estimates exploration coverage. Across 54 evaluated applications, five frontier systems reach at most 0.530 weighted fidelity and 22.9% fully reproduced requirements under application-equal averaging. These descriptive results expose both exploration-evidence gaps and implementation shortfalls. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nologistic/recreateanything.

papers.title: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining
papers.authors: Yingqi Shi, Junru Lu, Yun Liu, Di Yin et al.
papers.summary: Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.

papers.title: ZoionNET: Low-Power Animal Intrusion Detection Using an Acoustic Deep-Learning Classifier for a Cellular Remote-Sensing System
papers.authors: Prasanna Vijay, Adarsh Gupta, Vansh Panwar, Vatsalya Singh et al.
papers.summary: Crop raiding and village intrusion by elephants and large felids impose a recurring cost on communities along forest boundaries in southern India, and existing camera-based monitoring has proven difficult to sustain on the power budgets available at such sites. We present ZoionNET, a battery-powered sensing node that detects animal intrusion acoustically rather than visually. Audio from an onboard PDM microphone is sampled at 8 kHz, converted to mel-spectrograms on-device, and classified on an Arm Ethos-U55 microNPU by two int8-quantised YOLOv8 models arranged as a two-state machine: a lightweight always-on model runs in a dormant state and gates a four-class species classifier through exponential-moving-average thresholds, so the heavier model runs only when an intrusion is likely. A digital vibration sensor supplies a complementary seismic channel. Inferences leave the node as JSON over a cellular Notecard, reaching a web dashboard and SMS alerts to forest rangers without any local gateway. The two models reach reported accuracies of 0.974 and 0.946 on held-out audio, and a complete node costs USD 133.57 in parts. We report the system as built and deployed, and identify explicitly what has not yet been measured, most notably the energy behaviour that motivates the two-state design.

papers.title: Streaming-AAA: Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency
papers.authors: Zhihao Hu, Jianqi Ma, Jun Zhang, Jiayang Bai et al.
papers.summary: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.

papers.title: Presenting Your Figures: Data-informed Animated Transitions Across Scientific Figure Panels
papers.authors: Lu Ying, Can Liu, Yuxiao Yang, Jianing Yin et al.
papers.summary: Multi-panel figures are commonly used in research papers to show scientific data, and researchers often reuse them when presenting their work. Presenting these figures often involves explaining how data across chart panels are related. Animated transitions can progressively reveal these relationships, but two static panels specify only the endpoints, leaving what intermediate keyframes should show and how the transition should progress unclear. To support transition design across diverse scientific figures, we developed Figure Space and Transition Space through iterative analysis of 48 published multi-panel figures across eight scientific subject areas. Figure Space represents panel composition, data transformations, and visual encodings while retaining the links needed to trace panel results back to records. Transition Space uses this representation and source data to construct and sequence keyframes that make corresponding data visible and align them while preserving the meaning of each panel's position encodings. Building on these spaces, we developed FigFlux, a human-in-the-loop authoring system that guides AI agents in generating animated transitions from a multi-panel figure and its associated materials. Researchers can revise keyframes in natural language before animation generation. We evaluate FigFlux through cross-domain case studies, a study with 16 scientific authors, and expert assessment. Authors reported lower overall workload than with their familiar tools, while experts gave FigFlux transitions higher ratings than transitions created with participants' familiar tools or generated by AI alone. The example gallery have been published online: https://figflux.github.io.

papers.title: Blind tests of a simple-body model of submarine target strength on open benchmarks
papers.authors: Sunil Tyagi
papers.summary: Finite-element and boundary-element models of a submarine's sonar echo need a mesh and a solver, and their cost grows quickly with frequency. SSR-Sim takes an analytical route. The hull is cut into a few simple bodies, the echo of each is a closed-form result of geometrical acoustics or of the Kirchhoff approximation, the surface enters through a plane-wave reflection coefficient, and the echoes add in energy. This paper describes the method, including the reduction of a hull and its sail to simple bodies, and tests it on three open cases. (1) The reflection coefficient of a 50 mm rubber tile on steel plating, computed with finite elements by Yang et al., is reproduced to 0.02 rms or better at incidence angles from 0° to 75° once the layer is allowed to refract. (2) For the rigid full-scale BeTSSi submarine at 1 kHz, a prediction fixed before the reference was opened agrees with the boundary-element results of Venås and Kvamsdal to within 0.7 dB in every aspect sector from the bow to 150°; in the stern sector it is 5 dB high. (3) For a 1:15 BeTSSi model with 10 mm tiles measured in a lake, a second blind prediction is within -3.1, +1.4 and -0.5 dB of the measured level over aspects 0-120° at 5, 15 and 20 kHz, against -3.1, +3.1 and +3.5 dB for the Kirchhoff-finite-element computation published with the measurement. At 10 kHz, on a resonance of the tile, the prediction is 6.9 dB low, and in the bow sector it is 7 dB or more low at every frequency. The tests cover the specular component and the coating model only. The failures show what such a model lacks: edge diffraction and the returns that set the off-beam floor of a real model.
